questions.q: What is Node.js, in the lesson's framing?
options: A runtime that runs JavaScript outside a browser, with built-in modules for the OS
questions.explain: It's the node executable plus built-in modules for files, sockets, processes, timers and cryptography.

questions.q: What does V8 do, and what does libuv do?
options: V8 handles I/O; libuv runs JavaScript
V8 executes JavaScript; libuv provides the event loop and asynchronous OS access
questions.explain: V8 knows nothing about files or networks.

questions.q: A setTimeout of 10 ms is queued, then a 500 ms busy loop runs. Roughly when does the timer fire?
options: After the loop, around 504 ms, because the thread was busy
questions.explain: The event loop only checks timers once the current JavaScript finishes.

questions.q: What is the 'good consequence' of one main thread?
options: No locks or data races on your objects
questions.explain: The bad one: a long-running function makes everything else wait.

questions.q: Which Node major versions become LTS?
questions.explain: Odd-numbered majors are Current only and are abandoned after a few months.

questions.q: What does `node -p "process.release.lts"` print on a Current build?
options: undefined (on LTS builds it prints the codename)
questions.explain: It reveals whether you're running an LTS build.

questions.q: Why is a version manager recommended over the official installer?
options: It installs versions in your home directory and switches per shell or project, with no sudo
It's the only way to get npm
questions.explain: The installer is fine for a single version, but upgrades mean reinstalling and global packages may need sudo.

questions.q: What should you use for servers and anything you deploy?
options: An Active or Maintenance LTS version
questions.explain: Check github.com/nodejs/release for the schedule.

questions.q: How does Node decide a .js file's module type?
options: The nearest package.json: "type": "module" means ESM; commonjs or no type means CommonJS
questions.explain: *.mjs is always ESM and *.cjs always CommonJS.

questions.q: What must relative imports include in ESM?
questions.explain: ESM resolution doesn't guess extensions or look for index.js.

questions.q: What replaces __dirname and __filename in ESM?
options: import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename, or import.meta.url with new URL()
questions.explain: require is also unavailable by default.

questions.q: What does a dynamic import('./math.mjs') return?
questions.explain: Top-level await also works in ESM.

questions.q: What does ^5.1.0 accept?
questions.explain: ~5.1.0 accepts patches only; for 0.x versions, caret is stricter (^0.4.2 means >=0.4.2 <0.5.0).

questions.q: How does `npm ci` differ from `npm install`?
options: It installs exactly what the lockfile says, deletes node_modules first, and fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree
questions.explain: Use it in CI and Docker builds for reproducibility.

questions.q: What does "private": true prevent?
options: An accidental npm publish of an application
questions.explain: It's typical for applications.

questions.q: Why have devDependencies?
options: They're only needed to develop, test or build, and `npm ci --omit=dev` skips them, shrinking container images
questions.explain: dependencies are needed at runtime.

questions.q: Which fs style is the default for application code and servers?
questions.explain: *Sync suits startup code, CLIs and build scripts, where blocking is harmless.

questions.q: Why prefer attempting the operation and handling errors over checking first with access?
options: Another process can change the file between the check and the use (a TOCTOU race)
questions.explain: Handle errors by code, such as ENOENT, and rethrow real problems like EACCES.

questions.q: What does mkdir('data/cache', { recursive: true }) do?
options: Like mkdir -p: creates parents and doesn't error if it exists
questions.explain: rm with recursive and force is like rm -rf — careful.

questions.q: When should you use createReadStream?
options: For large files, or to start processing before the whole file is in memory
questions.explain: readFile loads the whole file.

questions.q: What is the error-first callback convention?
options: The last argument is a callback whose first parameter is an error (or null)
The first argument is a callback
questions.explain: For example fs.readFile(file, enc, (err, text) => ...).

questions.q: Why can't a try/catch around the original call catch an exception thrown inside a callback?
options: The stack has already unwound by the time the callback runs
questions.explain: That's one of the problems with callbacks, alongside the callback pyramid.

questions.q: What does util.promisify do?
options: Converts an error-first callback function into a promise-returning one
questions.explain: Many built-ins also have promise versions such as node:fs/promises.

questions.q: Why wrap errors with new Error(msg, { cause: err })?
options: It preserves the original root cause for logs
questions.explain: Use it when rethrowing with more context.

questions.q: In the order queue example, when does `added #1` print relative to `before add` and `after add`?
options: Between them, because emit is synchronous
questions.explain: Listeners run synchronously inside emit.

questions.q: What happens if an EventEmitter emits 'error' with no listener?
options: The error is thrown and can crash the process
questions.explain: That's why the example registers q.on('error', …) — the 'error' event is special.

questions.q: Why did 'queue full - flushing' print only once even though the queue stayed full?
options: It was registered with once, which removes the listener after one call
questions.explain: The listener count for 'added' stayed at 1.

questions.q: What does events.once(emitter, name) return?
options: A promise for the next event, resolving to an array of its arguments
questions.explain: It's the cleanest way to await something like a 'ready' event.

questions.q: What are req and res in node:http?
options: req is a readable stream (IncomingMessage); res is a writable stream (ServerResponse)
questions.explain: req.url holds the path and query string only.

questions.q: What happens if you forget res.end()?
options: The client hangs until it times out
questions.explain: Always end every response path.

questions.q: Why does readJsonBody cap the body size at MAX_BODY?
options: To reject oversized bodies with 413 instead of buffering unbounded input
questions.explain: Invalid JSON returns 400.

questions.q: How is the query string read in the example?
options: With new URL(req.url, base) and url.searchParams.get('q')
questions.explain: The pathname is matched with regexes such as /^\/notes\/(\d+)$/.

questions.q: What type are process.env values?
questions.explain: process.env.X = 1 stores '1', and assigning undefined stores 'undefined'.

questions.q: Which takes precedence: a variable in the real environment or one in the .env file?
questions.explain: On a test run, PORT=5000 node --env-file=.env app.js used 5000, not the file's 4000.

questions.q: How do current Node releases load .env files?
options: Natively with --env-file or process.loadEnvFile(), no dotenv needed
questions.explain: --env-file-if-exists is available for optional files.

questions.q: Why centralise and validate configuration in one module?
options: A typo then fails at startup instead of giving undefined at 3 a.m.
questions.explain: It also shows what a service needs at a glance.

questions.q: What do logstat's exit codes mean?
options: 0 success, 1 runtime failure (e.g. unreadable file), 2 usage error
questions.explain: Conventional exit codes make a CLI scriptable.

questions.q: How does logstat handle files larger than memory?
options: It processes line by line via readline and async iteration
questions.explain: It also reads standard input when no file is given, so cat *.log | logstat works.

questions.q: What does the bin entry in package.json do?
options: Maps a command name to a file; npm link or npm install -g puts an executable on your PATH
questions.explain: The entry is { "logstat": "./bin/logstat.js" }.

questions.q: Why keep parsing and statistics as pure functions?
options: They're easy to test and reuse; only the bin file touches process
questions.explain: parse.js and stats.js do no I/O.

questions.q: Which Express 5 change affects async handlers?
options: Rejected promises from async handlers are forwarded to error handlers automatically
questions.explain: Another change: req.body is undefined, not {}, when no body parser ran.

questions.q: What does express.json() replace from the raw http version?
questions.explain: res.json replaces sendJson, and app.get replaces the if chain.

questions.q: What type are values in req.params?
questions.explain: /books/:id gives { id: '42' }.

questions.q: What is in req.body without a body-parsing middleware?
questions.explain: Mount express.json() to parse JSON bodies.

questions.q: What distinguishes middleware from a route handler?
options: Both are (req, res, next); middleware calls next() to pass control on
questions.explain: Auth, logging, CORS, rate limiting and body parsing all look the same: functions in a pipeline.

questions.q: In what order does middleware run?
options: In the order registered, only for matching mount paths
questions.explain: The lesson's order: helmet, json, logger, /admin guard, routers, 404, error handler.

questions.q: What is the shape of Express error-handling middleware?
options: Four arguments (err, req, res, next), registered last
questions.explain: The notFoundHandler comes just before it.

questions.q: What changed in Express 5 route paths?
options: Wildcards must be named, like /files/*filepath, and regex characters are no longer special
questions.explain: Old '/files/*' or '/:id?' forms need updating; use {/:section} for optional segments.

questions.q: Which pair is correct for creating a resource?
options: POST /tasks returns 201 with a Location header
questions.explain: Model nouns as resources and let HTTP methods be the verbs.

questions.q: Which methods are idempotent?
questions.explain: POST is neither safe nor idempotent, so retrying a create-payment POST is dangerous without idempotency keys.

questions.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
options: 401: not authenticated; 403: authenticated but not allowed
questions.explain: 404 means no such resource.

questions.q: What is the difference between PATCH and PUT?
options: PATCH sends only the fields to change; PUT sends the whole representation
questions.explain: With PUT, missing fields mean remove or reset.

questions.q: Why validate input at the edge?
options: So the rest of the code can trust its inputs' shape, or the client gets a clear 400
questions.explain: Anything arriving over HTTP is untrusted, even an added "isAdmin": true.

questions.q: What did CreateUser.parse({ email, name: '  Ada ', age: '36' }) return?
options: A new object: name trimmed to 'Ada', age coerced to 36, defaults added (role 'member', tags [])
questions.explain: Use the parsed output, not the original input.

questions.q: How does safeParse differ from parse?
options: It returns { success, data } or { success: false, error } instead of throwing a ZodError
questions.explain: It's easier to turn into an HTTP response.

questions.q: Why does a Zod schema count as 'one declaration, three benefits'?
options: Runtime validation, parsing (coercion, trimming, defaults), and a static TypeScript type
questions.explain: Alternatives include Valibot, ArkType, Joi, Yup and Ajv.

questions.q: What is an operational error?
options: An expected failure of a correct program, such as bad JSON, a missing record or a dropped DB connection
questions.explain: You handle these with a 4xx, a retry or degraded behaviour.

questions.q: What should you do for a programmer error (a bug) outside any request?
options: Let the process crash and be restarted, since state may be inconsistent
questions.explain: For a bug inside a request, return 500, log loudly, and fix the code.

questions.q: What does the errorHandler return to the client for status ≥ 500?
options: A generic 'internal server error', not the real message
questions.explain: The details go to the log, not the client.

questions.q: Why check res.headersSent in the error handler?
options: If a response has already started, delegate to the default handler with next(err)
questions.explain: You can't send a second response.

questions.q: What do pg and Kysely each do?
options: Kysely is the driver; pg is the builder
pg is the driver (wire protocol and connection pool); Kysely is a type-safe query builder on top
questions.explain: Kysely compiles to parameterized SQL and keeps you close to SQL.

questions.q: How many Kysely instances (pools) should a process create?
options: One per process at startup, with db.destroy() on shutdown
questions.explain: Pass it to your routers.

questions.q: What are migrations?
options: Versioned scripts applied in order and recorded in a table so each runs once
questions.explain: Kysely's Migrator runs files exporting up (and optionally down).

questions.q: What is PGlite used for in the lesson?
options: A WebAssembly build of Postgres inside Node, handy for tests
questions.explain: It's used for the Level 2 project's tests.

questions.q: Why not store a plain fast hash like SHA-256 of a password?
options: Attackers can guess billions of candidates per second on GPUs after a leak
questions.explain: Use a deliberately slow, salted, memory-hard function: argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt.

questions.q: Why does hashing the same password twice give different results?
options: A new random salt is generated each time
questions.explain: The lesson shows (await hashPassword(p)) === stored is false.

questions.q: Why use timingSafeEqual when comparing hashes?
options: To avoid leaking information via comparison timing
questions.explain: Cost parameters are stored with each hash so they can be raised later.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication is who is making the request; authorization is whether they may do that
questions.explain: Authorization is usually plain code like where user_id = req.user.id.

questions.q: What does the built-in node:test runner need?
options: No test framework dependency at all (with node:assert)
questions.explain: Add Supertest for HTTP-level tests without opening a real port.

questions.q: Which test layer gives the best confidence per test for an API?
options: Integration tests through HTTP, covering routing, validation, middleware, SQL and serialization together
questions.explain: Keep unit tests for logic with many edge cases.

questions.q: In the retry test where the function fails twice then succeeds, how many calls are made?
questions.explain: callCount() is 3 and the result is 'finally'.

questions.q: What does assert.rejects check?
options: That an async function rejects with the expected error
That a value is rejected by a filter
questions.explain: The give-up test expects the last error to be rethrown.

questions.q: Why use structured JSON logs rather than console.log strings in production?
options: Machines can filter and aggregate fields, e.g. every error for request b7e1c2
questions.explain: One JSON object per line with consistent fields.

questions.q: What is the Pino call signature?
options: logger.level(mergingObject, message), with data in the object and a constant message
questions.explain: A constant message ('order placed') lets you count occurrences, while orderId stays queryable.

questions.q: What does the redact option do?
options: Replaces sensitive paths such as *.password with [redacted] in log output
questions.explain: The example censors req.headers.authorization, *.password and card.number.

questions.q: At level 'info', what happens to logger.debug(...)?
options: It's dropped; levels are numbers (debug 20, info 30)
questions.explain: trace 10, debug 20, info 30, warn 40, error 50, fatal 60.

questions.q: What should the API return when a user requests another user's task?
options: 404, not 403, so it doesn't reveal that the task exists
questions.explain: Users can never read or modify another user's tasks.

questions.q: What are the project's lifetime and format for access tokens?
options: A JWT access token valid for 15 minutes, sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>
questions.explain: Registration and login return it.

questions.q: Which status codes does the project use for validation errors, duplicates and unknown routes?
options: 400 with per-field details, 409, and a JSON 404
questions.explain: Bugs return a 500 without internals.

questions.q: How does the test suite run against a real Postgres engine without a server?
options: PGlite via a test-only in-process pool adapter
questions.explain: It's driven with Supertest.

questions.q: Which two queues are drained after every single callback, in every phase?
options: The process.nextTick queue, then the microtask queue
questions.explain: The loop advances only when both are empty.

questions.q: Inside an I/O (fs) callback, which runs first: setImmediate or setTimeout(fn, 0)?
options: setImmediate, because the check phase follows the poll phase
questions.explain: Verified: 'immediate inside I/O' printed before 'timeout inside I/O'. From the main module their order can vary.

questions.q: Why could a recursive process.nextTick freeze a server?
options: The nextTick queue is drained completely before the loop proceeds, so it starves I/O
It blocks the thread permanently by design
questions.explain: The same applies to microtasks queuing microtasks.

questions.q: In which phase do setImmediate callbacks run?
questions.explain: Timers handle setTimeout and setInterval; poll waits for I/O.

questions.q: What does write() returning false mean?
options: The internal buffer is full; stop until the 'drain' event
questions.explain: It's advisory: nothing forces you to stop, but ignoring it piles data up in memory.

questions.q: What does highWaterMark control?
options: How many bytes can be buffered before write() returns false
questions.explain: It bounds memory regardless of how slow the consumer is.

questions.q: Which stream type is zlib.createGzip()?
questions.explain: Transform streams derive output from input; Duplex has independent sides, like a TCP socket.

questions.q: What helper handles backpressure for you so you rarely write the drain loop by hand?
questions.explain: The hand-written loop shows how it works.

questions.q: Buffer.from('héllo €', 'utf8') has what length versus the string's length?
questions.explain: é is 2 bytes and € is 3 bytes. Use Buffer.byteLength(str) for Content-Length, never str.length.

questions.q: Does Buffer.subarray copy memory?
options: No: it shares memory, so changing the view changes the original
questions.explain: Buffer.from(buffer) makes an independent copy.

questions.q: What goes wrong when a chunk boundary falls inside the multi-byte character €?
options: toString() on each chunk yields replacement characters; StringDecoder holds back incomplete sequences
questions.explain: setEncoding('utf8') on a stream does this internally.

questions.q: What is base64url used for?
options: URL-safe base64 without padding, as in JWTs
questions.explain: Buffer is a subclass of Uint8Array.

questions.q: When do you use worker_threads versus child_process?
options: worker_threads for CPU-bound JavaScript in the same process; child_process for external programs or strong isolation
questions.explain: Each worker has its own V8 isolate and event loop.

questions.q: Why does heavy computation on the main thread hurt a server?
options: It blocks the event loop, so every other request waits
questions.explain: The lesson's heartbeat counter shows the main thread stalling.

questions.q: How do the main thread and a worker communicate?
questions.explain: The worker posts { id, result } back.

questions.q: What do four workers running four jobs achieve?
options: True parallelism across CPU cores while the main thread stays free
questions.explain: The comparison measured heartbeats during each run.

questions.q: Why run several copies of a Node process?
options: One process uses one core, so an 8-core server stays mostly idle once request handling is the bottleneck
questions.explain: Two ways: node:cluster, or N replicas behind a load balancer as containers and Kubernetes do.

questions.q: How are requests distributed in the lesson's three-worker demo?
options: Round-robin across workers, and the primary replaces a worker that dies
questions.explain: The port stays open throughout because the primary owns it.

questions.q: What does clustering not give you?
options: Shared memory: each worker has its own heap, so in-memory caches, rate-limit counters and sessions exist per worker
questions.explain: Use Redis or another shared store.

questions.q: What does worker.disconnect() on SIGTERM do?
options: Lets workers finish in-flight requests, then exit
questions.explain: exitedAfterDisconnect tells the primary it was intentional, so it doesn't fork a replacement.

questions.q: What is the cache-aside pattern?
options: On read, try the cache, load from the database on a miss and store with a TTL; on write, update the database and delete the cache key
questions.explain: Deleting is safer than updating the cached value.

questions.q: What is the downside of in-process caches compared with Redis?
options: Each process has its own copy, it's lost on restart, and it competes with your heap
questions.explain: Redis is shared by all processes and survives app restarts.

questions.q: Why must the node-redis client have an 'error' listener?
options: It's an EventEmitter, and an unhandled 'error' would crash the process on a Redis blip
questions.explain: The client reconnects automatically.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the Redis calls it shows?
options: They were checked against the package's type definitions but not run; the cache logic was run against an in-memory stand-in
questions.explain: The lesson is honest about what was verified.

questions.q: What do WebSockets provide beyond HTTP?
options: A long-lived full-duplex connection where either side can send at any time
questions.explain: Useful for chat, live dashboards and multiplayer games.

questions.q: When is Server-Sent Events (SSE) enough?
options: For one-way server-to-client streams like notifications and dashboards, with browser auto-reconnect
questions.explain: It's a plain HTTP response that stays open.

questions.q: What does the heartbeat with ping and terminate do?
options: Detects and terminates connections that stop answering (dead NAT paths, sleeping laptops)
questions.explain: A socket is marked not alive until it answers pong.

questions.q: Why does the server set maxPayload and close with 1007 for invalid JSON?
options: To bound memory per message and reject malformed input
questions.explain: Binary frames are closed with 1003 'text only'.

questions.q: Why not use the client's filename on disk?
options: It may be something like ../../app/server.js; generate your own name (e.g. randomUUID)
questions.explain: The diskStorage filename callback returns randomUUID().

questions.q: How should you check an uploaded file's type?
options: Check the actual bytes (magic-number signatures), not the client-supplied mimetype or extension
questions.explain: For example PNG starts with 89 50 4e 47 and JPEG with ff d8 ff.

questions.q: Why doesn't express.json() work for file uploads?
options: Multipart bodies need a streaming multipart parser such as multer (built on busboy)
questions.explain: The body has parts separated by a boundary string.

questions.q: Which limits does the example set?
options: fileSize 2 MB, one file and five fields
questions.explain: Limits prevent enormous uploads; production systems often upload directly to object storage.

questions.q: What is broken access control in a Node API?
options: GET /tasks/:id returning any user's task; defend by scoping every query by owner
questions.explain: It's the first OWASP category.

questions.q: What does helmet() do?
options: Sets security headers such as content-security-policy and x-content-type-options
questions.explain: The lesson checks that the headers appear on a response.

questions.q: What does rateLimit({ windowMs: 60_000, limit: 5 }) on /auth/login do?
options: Allows 5 requests per minute per client, slowing credential guessing
questions.explain: No rate limit on login is an 'insecure design' example.

questions.q: How do you defend against SSRF, where the server fetches a user-supplied URL?
questions.explain: Also use execFile rather than exec for injection defense.

questions.q: How does the chat server authenticate connections?
options: During the upgrade, with a signed expiring token and an Origin check
questions.explain: Tokens are short-lived and issued by the Express app.

questions.q: How are client messages validated?
options: With a Zod discriminated union keyed by type (join, leave, say, typing)
questions.explain: Anything else is rejected before it reaches the room logic.

questions.q: What protects against slow consumers?
questions.explain: Each connection also has a token-bucket rate limit.

questions.q: Why does the Rooms state need pub/sub to scale out?
options: It's in-memory for one process, so other processes wouldn't see it
questions.explain: Graceful shutdown uses close code 1001.

questions.q: What is the most time-saving rule of performance work?
options: Profile before optimizing; the slow part is rarely where you expect
questions.explain: Guessing at causes wastes days.

questions.q: How does V8's sampling CPU profiler work?
options: Roughly every millisecond it records the current JavaScript call stack; functions in many samples are where CPU time goes
questions.explain: Collect with node --cpu-prof, or --inspect with Chrome DevTools.

questions.q: What does `node --cpu-prof` write?
options: A .cpuprofile file when the process exits
questions.explain: It's JSON, viewable as a flame chart in DevTools.

questions.q: What were the two hidden inefficiencies in buildReport?
options: A missing await and a missing cache
A memory leak and a deadlock
Re-sorting the whole array for every order, and JSON round-trips to copy objects
questions.explain: The report of 3000 orders took about 910 ms.

questions.q: What is a Node diagnostic report?
options: A JSON snapshot of the process: versions, stacks, heap stats, resource usage and every libuv handle
questions.explain: process.report.getReport() generates one on demand.

questions.q: How do you get a report from a hung process without killing it?
options: Run with --report-on-signal and send SIGUSR2: kill -USR2 <pid>
questions.explain: The libuv section then shows open sockets and timers.

questions.q: What did the lesson find when --report-directory pointed to a missing directory?
options: Node printed 'Failed to open Node.js report file' and wrote nothing
questions.explain: The directory must already exist.

questions.q: Why treat diagnostic reports as sensitive?
options: They contain environment variables, potentially secrets
questions.explain: Newer versions can exclude them with --report-exclude-env.

questions.q: What two separate jobs does TypeScript tooling do?
options: Type checking (tsc) and producing runnable JavaScript (removing annotations)
questions.explain: Current Node can strip types itself when you run node file.ts; type checking remains tsc's job.

questions.q: Why must imports use './money.ts' with the extension when running .ts directly?
options: Node resolves the file exactly as written (ESM rules)
questions.explain: The type modifier (import { type Money }) marks an import as erased at runtime.

questions.q: What does `node src/main.ts` print for add($19.99, $5.00) in the lesson?
questions.explain: Amounts are integer minor units: 1999 + 500 = 2499 cents.

questions.q: Why store money as integer minor units?
options: To avoid floating-point errors with currency
questions.explain: The format function divides by 100 for display.

questions.q: In the layered architecture, what belongs in route handlers?
options: HTTP translation only: parse and validate input, call a service, shape the response
questions.explain: Services hold business rules with no req/res; repositories hold data access.

questions.q: Why should services take plain arguments and return plain values?
options: So a CLI, a queue worker or a test can call them too
questions.explain: They contain no req or res.

questions.q: In hexagonal architecture, who defines ports and who implements them?
options: The core defines ports (interfaces it needs); adapters implement them
Adapters define ports; the core implements
questions.explain: Dependency arrows all point inward.

questions.q: What does this make easier?
options: Testing the core with in-memory adapters, and swapping infrastructure
questions.explain: The core imports nothing from Express, Kysely or an SDK.

questions.q: Why move slow work (emails, PDFs, image resizing) out of the request?
options: Doing it inline slows responses, ties latency to third-party reliability, and loses work on a restart
questions.explain: The request enqueues a job and returns, often 202 Accepted.

questions.q: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do in the Postgres queue?
options: Lets multiple workers claim different jobs without waiting on rows another worker has locked
questions.explain: pg-boss and Graphile Worker build on the same technique.

questions.q: Which is the most widely used Node job library on Redis?
questions.explain: It offers delays, retries, priorities, rate limits and repeatable jobs.

questions.q: What happens to a job that keeps failing past max_attempts?
options: It ends in a 'dead' status for inspection
questions.explain: Statuses: queued, running, done, dead.

questions.q: What must every service-to-service HTTP call have?
options: A timeout, so a hung dependency doesn't hang you
questions.explain: Also bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker and propagated request ids.

questions.q: What does the lesson's circuit breaker do after `threshold` consecutive failures?
options: Fails fast for coolDownMs, then allows one trial request (half-open)
questions.explain: It stops a dead dependency from consuming resources.

questions.q: Which statuses are treated as retryable?
questions.explain: Only transient failures should be retried.

questions.q: What does the lesson caution about microservices?
options: Many teams are better served by a modular monolith until organisational or scaling pressure justifies splitting
questions.explain: Every in-process call becomes a network call that can be slow or fail.

questions.q: Why copy package manifests before the source in a Dockerfile?
options: So the npm ci layer is cached and only re-runs when dependencies change
questions.explain: npm ci --omit=dev installs exactly the lockfile without test tools.

questions.q: Why USER node?
options: A compromised process shouldn't be root inside the container
questions.explain: Official images include an unprivileged node user.

questions.q: What does the lesson honestly say about its Dockerfile?
options: It is a Docker Compose file
It was written for Docker but not built or run, because the authoring machine had no container runtime
questions.explain: Build it yourself and fix anything your environment disagrees with.

questions.q: How do -slim and -alpine images differ?
options: -slim is Debian-based without compilers; -alpine is smaller but uses musl libc, which some native modules don't support well
questions.explain: Distroless images are smaller still, with no shell.

questions.q: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
options: Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability lets you ask why without shipping new code
questions.explain: It rests on logs, metrics and traces.

questions.q: What do traces show?
options: The path of one request through services as a tree of timed spans
questions.explain: They answer 'which of the 14 calls behind this slow request was slow?'.

questions.q: What is OpenTelemetry?
options: A vendor-neutral standard for producing logs, metrics and traces, exported over OTLP to a collector
questions.explain: Route data to Jaeger, Grafana, Honeycomb, Datadog and so on.

questions.q: Why does instrumentation live in its own file loaded with --import?
options: It must load before the app imports the modules it patches, and ESM needs a loader hook via register()
questions.explain: For CommonJS require it's easy to intercept; ESM needs the hook.

questions.q: What does a platform send when it stops an instance, and what can't be caught?
options: SIGTERM, then after a grace period SIGKILL, which can't be caught
questions.explain: A good service finishes within the grace period.

questions.q: What is the first step of the shutdown sequence?
options: Stop being ready (e.g. /readyz returns 503) so the load balancer stops sending new requests
questions.explain: Then server.close(), finish in-flight work, close idle keep-alives, close resources in order, and exit.

questions.q: Why set a hard deadline timer with unref()?
options: So the process never hangs forever, without keeping the event loop alive on its own
questions.explain: Keep it below the platform's kill timeout.

questions.q: In what order should resources close?
options: In order, such as DB pools, Redis, message consumers, then telemetry exporters (to flush buffered spans and logs)
questions.explain: The example uses a db.end() step.

questions.q: Which key constraint does the Bookings capstone highlight?
options: Two overlapping bookings for the same resource must be impossible, even under concurrent requests
questions.explain: Constraints in the database enforce invariants.

questions.q: When should the confirmation email job be enqueued?
options: When a booking is created, in the same transaction
questions.explain: A reminder job runs 30 minutes before the start.

questions.q: How should the utilization report be computed?
options: Without blocking the event loop, whatever the date range
questions.explain: It draws on worker threads and streaming ideas from Level 3.

questions.q: What shape should the domain and use cases have?
options: Independent of Express and the DB, with a composition root
questions.explain: The non-functional table also requires TypeScript strict, Zod at boundaries and one error format.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```javascript
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events'
const e = new EventEmitter()
e.on('x', () => console.log('A'))
e.once('x', () => console.log('B'))
console.log('start')
console.log(e.emit('x'))
console.log(e.emit('x'))
console.log(e.emit('nobody'), e.listenerCount('x'))
```
options: start, true, A, B, A, true, false 1
start, A, B, true, A, B, true, false 2
A, B, start, true, A, true, false 1
start, A, B, true, A, true, false 1 (one per line)
questions.explain: emit is synchronous, so listeners run before emit returns true. The once listener is removed after the first call. emit returns false with no listeners, and one listener remains.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```javascript
console.log(Buffer.from('héllo €').length, 'héllo €'.length, Buffer.byteLength('€'))
```
questions.explain: In UTF-8, é takes 2 bytes and € takes 3, so the string has 7 characters but 10 bytes.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```javascript
const b = Buffer.from('abcdef')
const v = b.subarray(0, 3); v[0] = 0x5a
console.log(b.toString())
const c = Buffer.from(b); c[0] = 0x71
console.log(b.toString(), c.toString())
```
questions.explain: subarray shares memory with the original, but Buffer.from(buffer) makes an independent copy.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```javascript
process.env.N = 5
console.log(typeof process.env.N, process.env.N, process.env.NOPE)
```
questions.explain: Values in process.env are always strings (or undefined when missing).

questions.q:
In what order are these lines printed?
```javascript
async function f() { console.log('f1'); await null; console.log('f2') }
f()
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('p1'))
console.log('sync')
```
questions.explain: f runs synchronously up to its first await; the continuation is queued as a microtask before the .then callback, so f2 prints before p1.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```javascript
const r = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject(new Error('no')), 3])
console.log(r.map(x => x.status).join(','))
```
questions.explain: allSettled never rejects: it reports each outcome. Promise.all would reject on the first failure.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```javascript
console.log(path.join('/srv/app', 'uploads', '../logs', 'app.log'), path.basename('/a/b/c.txt', '.txt'), path.extname('x.tar.gz'))
```
questions.explain: path.join normalises '..', basename strips the given extension, and extname returns only the last extension.

questions.q:
What does this print?
```javascript
const u = new URL('/notes?q=Tea&q=Milk&limit=5', 'http://localhost')
console.log(u.pathname, u.searchParams.get('q'), u.searchParams.getAll('q').length, Number(u.searchParams.get('limit')) + 1)
```
questions.explain: get returns the first value, getAll returns all of them, and query values are strings, so limit needs Number().

questions.q: Which of these does the range ^5.1.0 accept, and which does ^0.4.2 accept? (5.9.1, 6.0.0 against ^5.1.0; 0.4.9, 0.5.0 against ^0.4.2)
questions.explain: Caret allows changes that don't bump the leftmost non-zero part, so for 0.x versions a minor bump may break.

questions.q:
What does this pipeline produce?
```javascript
const out = []
await pipeline(
  Readable.from(['a', 'b', 'c']),
  new Transform({ transform(ch, enc, cb) { cb(null, ch.toString().toUpperCase()) } }),
  async function (src) { for await (const x of src) out.push(x.toString()) },
)
console.log(out.join(''))
```
questions.explain: Transform maps each chunk to upper case; pipeline wires the streams and handles backpressure and errors.

questions.q: A server hashes passwords with scrypt and a random salt per password. For the same password, are two stored hashes equal?
options: Yes if the cost is the same
No: a different random salt gives a different hash, so compare with the stored salt and timingSafeEqual
questions.explain: The same password and the same salt gives equal output (verified by running), but a fresh salt does not.

questions.q: What delays does exponential backoff with base 100 ms give for four retries?
questions.explain: base × 2^i. Add jitter so many clients don't retry at the same instant.

questions.q:
A circuit breaker has threshold 3. The calls fail, fail, fail, then succeed, succeed. What are the results?
(breaker returns 'open' while failures ≥ threshold)
questions.explain: After three consecutive failures it fails fast until the cool-down, even though the dependency may have recovered (the simulated breaker has no cool-down here).

questions.q: Why does a 500 ms CPU-bound loop make a 10 ms timer fire at about 500 ms?
options: Node runs JavaScript on one main thread, so the event loop can only check timers when the current code finishes
questions.explain: Move CPU-heavy work to worker_threads.

questions.q: Inside an fs callback, which runs first: setImmediate or setTimeout(fn, 0)?
options: setImmediate, because the check phase follows the poll phase
questions.explain: Verified by running: 'immediate inside I/O' printed before 'timeout inside I/O'.

questions.q: What should a service do on SIGTERM?
options: Report not ready, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources, then exit before SIGKILL
questions.explain: SIGKILL can't be caught, so use a hard deadline timer.

questions.q: Why should file uploads be sniffed by bytes and renamed on disk?
options: The client's mimetype, extension and filename can lie or contain ../ paths; use magic numbers and a generated name
questions.explain: Also set size limits.

questions.q: How does Express recognise an error-handling middleware, and where is it registered?
options: It is named errorHandler and registered first
It has two parameters and runs before routes
It takes four parameters (err, req, res, next) and is registered last
questions.explain: Express 5 also forwards rejected promises from async handlers to it.

questions.q: A user asks for GET /tasks/17 owned by someone else. What should the API return, and why?
options: 404, so it doesn't reveal that the task exists, with the query scoped by owner
questions.explain: Scoping every query by the owner also prevents broken access control.

questions.q: You run three cluster workers and keep a Map as a rate-limit counter in each. What goes wrong?
options: Each worker has its own heap, so counters aren't shared; use a shared store such as Redis
questions.explain: Clustering doesn't give shared memory.

challenges.title: Retry with exponential backoff
challenges.prompt: Write an async function retry(fn, { attempts, baseMs }) that calls fn(i). If it throws, wait baseMs * 2**i ms (not after the last attempt) and try again. After the last attempt rethrow the last error. Track the waits and print them for a function that fails twice and then succeeds.
challenges.explain: Waits grow as base × 2^i, and the last attempt doesn't wait. Verified by running the solution in Node: output matches.

challenges.title: Parse access-log lines
challenges.prompt: Write parseLine(line) that matches the common log format and returns { method, path, status, bytes } or null for invalid lines. Then count requests by status class (2xx, 4xx…) for the sample lines.
challenges.explain: Keeping the parser a pure function makes it easy to test. A '-' byte count becomes 0. Verified by running the solution in Node: output matches.
